claim: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) could result in up to 10 million deaths annually by 2050.
source: As AMR has continued to spread and many antimicrobial agents have become ineffective against previously susceptible organisms, the World Health Organization recently projected that AMR could result in up to 10 million deaths annually by 2050 (Interagency Coordination Group on Antimicrobial Resistance, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to the Interagency Coordination Group on Antimicrobial Resistance, 2019.

claim: β-Lactam antibiotics constitute more than 65% of all injectable antibiotics in the United States.
source: Their cumulative use exceeds 65% of all injectable antibiotics in the United States (Bush and Bradford, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bush and Bradford, 2016.

claim: β-Lactam antibiotics work by inhibiting penicillin binding proteins (PBPs).
source: β-Lactam antibiotics work by inhibiting penicillin binding proteins (PBPs), a group of enzymes that catalyze transpeptidation and transglycosylation reactions that occur during the bacterial cell wall biosynthesis (Tooke et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tooke et al., 2019.

claim: The most common mechanism of resistance to β-lactam antibiotics in Gram-negative bacteria is the expression of β-lactamase enzymes.
source: Of the four primary mechanisms by which bacteria resist β-lactam antibiotics, the most common and important mechanism of resistance in Gram-negative bacteria, including common pathogens such as Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae, is the expression of β-lactamase enzymes (Tooke et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tooke et al., 2019.

claim: β-Lactamase enzymes hydrolyze the amide bond in the β-lactam ring.
source: These enzymes hydrolyze the amide bond in the β-lactam ring, resulting in a product that is incapable of inhibiting PBPs (Palzkill, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Palzkill, 2018.

claim: The Ambler system categorizes β-lactamase enzymes into classes A, B, C, and D based on amino acid sequence homology.
source: The Ambler system of classifying β-lactamase enzymes categorizes them, based on amino acid sequence homology, into classes A, B, C, and D (Ambler, 1980; Bush and Jacoby, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ambler, 1980 and Bush and Jacoby, 2010.

claim: β-Lactamases of classes A, C, and D are serine hydrolases.
source: While β-lactamases of classes A, C, and D are serine hydrolases, class B enzymes are metalloenzymes that have one or more zinc ions at the active site (Palzkill, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Palzkill, 2013.

claim: Class B β-lactamases are metalloenzymes that have one or more zinc ions at the active site.
source: While β-lactamases of classes A, C, and D are serine hydrolases, class B enzymes are metalloenzymes that have one or more zinc ions at the active site (Palzkill, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Palzkill, 2013.

claim: Class A enzymes are the most widely distributed and intensively studied of all β-lactamases.
source: Class A enzymes are the most widely distributed and intensively studied of all β-lactamases (Tooke et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tooke et al., 2019.

claim: The hydrolytic mechanism in class A β-lactamases is initiated by reversible binding of the antibiotic in the active site of the enzyme.
source: The hydrolytic mechanism in class A (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), revealed by experiments and QM/MM modeling, is initiated by reversible binding of the antibiotic in the active site of the enzyme (formation of the Michaelis complex).
evidence: The claim is supported by references to experiments and QM/MM modeling, and is illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Nucleophilic attack of the catalytic serine (Ser70) on the carbonyl carbon of the β-lactam ring results in a high-energy acylated intermediate.
source: This is followed by nucleophilic attack of the catalytic serine (Ser70) on the carbonyl carbon of the β-lactam ring, resulting in a high-energy acylated intermediate that quickly resolves, following protonation of the β-lactam nitrogen and cleavage of the C-N bond, to a lower energy covalent acyl-enzyme complex (Chudyk et al., 2014; Hermann et al., 2003; Hermann et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chudyk et al., 2014; Hermann et al., 2003; Hermann et al., 2005.

claim: An activated water molecule attacks the covalent complex, leading to hydrolysis of the bond between the β-lactam carbonyl and the serine oxygen.
source: Next, an activated water molecule attacks the covalent complex, leading to the subsequent hydrolysis of the bond between the β-lactam carbonyl and the serine oxygen, resulting in the regeneration of the active enzyme and release of the inactive β-lactam antibiotic (Tooke et al., 2019; Bonomo, 2017; Palzkill, 2018; Chudyk et al., 2014; Fisher and Mobashery, 2009; Hermann et al., 2006; Hirvonen et al., 2019; Pan et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations including Tooke et al., 2019; Bonomo, 2017; Palzkill, 2018; Chudyk et al., 2014; Fisher and Mobashery, 2009; Hermann et al., 2006; Hirvonen et al., 2019; Pan et al., 2017.

claim: TEM-1 is one of the most common plasmid-encoded β-lactamases in Gram-negative bacteria.
source: TEM-1 is one of the most common plasmid-encoded β-lactamases in Gram-negative bacteria and is a model class A enzyme (Brown et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Brown et al., 2009.

claim: TEM-1 has a narrow spectrum of hydrolytic activity limited to penicillins and early generation cephalosporins.
source: It has a narrow spectrum of hydrolytic activity that is limited to penicillins and early generation cephalosporins; in contrast, its activity toward large, inflexible, broad-spectrum oxyiminocephalosporins such as the widely used antibiotic ceftazidime is poor (Palzkill, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Palzkill, 2018.

claim: Mutations in the bla_TEM-1 gene have led to amino acid modifications that allow TEM-1 variants to hydrolyze broad-spectrum cephalosporins.
source: However, mutations in the bla_TEM-1 gene have led to amino acid modifications, which allow subsequent TEM-1 variants to hydrolyze broad-spectrum cephalosporins (so-called 'extended-spectrum' activity) or to avoid the action of mechanism-based inhibitors such as clavulanate that are used in combination with β-lactams to treat β-lactamase producing organisms (Brown et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Brown et al., 2009.

claim: KPC-2 is an extremely versatile β-lactamase with a broad spectrum of substrates that includes penicillins, cephamycins, and carbapenems.
source: Another class A enzyme, KPC-2 (K. pneumoniae carbapenemase-2), encoded by the bla_KPC-2 gene is an extremely versatile β-lactamase (Queenan et al., 2004) with a broad spectrum of substrates that includes penicillins, cephamycins, and, importantly, carbapenems (Queenan et al., 2004; Yigit et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Queenan et al., 2004 and Yigit et al., 2003.

claim: Class A β-lactamases share the same structural architecture despite sequence differences.
source: In spite of sequence differences, class A β-lactamases share the same structural architecture (Philippon et al., 2016), as evident from the present 47 structures of TEM-1 and 38 structures of KPC-2, or their engineered variants, deposited in the Protein Data Bank (PDB) at the time of this writing.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Philippon et al., 2016 and reference to PDB structures.

claim: The average mean order parameter (S2) for TEM-1, as calculated from NMR experiments, is between 0.81 and 0.94.
source: The average mean order parameter, S2, as calculated from NMR experiments for TEM-1, is between 0.81 and 0.94, and almost all class A β-lactamases are conformationally identical (Gobeil et al., 2019; Morin and Gagné, 2009; Savard and Gagné, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gobeil et al., 2019; Morin and Gagné, 2009; Savard and Gagné, 2006.

claim: Almost all class A β-lactamases are conformationally identical.
source: The average mean order parameter, S2, as calculated from NMR experiments for TEM-1, is between 0.81 and 0.94, and almost all class A β-lactamases are conformationally identical (Gobeil et al., 2019; Morin and Gagné, 2009; Savard and Gagné, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gobeil et al., 2019; Morin and Gagné, 2009; Savard and Gagné, 2006.

claim: Loops play a crucial role in the activity of many enzymes, including β-lactamases.
source: Loops (e.g. active site loops) play a crucial role in the activity of many enzymes (Liao et al., 2018), including β-lactamases.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Liao et al., 2018.

claim: Active site conformations in β-lactamases may be influenced by distal loops through networks of coupled motions.
source: There is increasing evidence that active site conformations may be influenced by distal loops, connected, for example, through active closure and desolvation, and potentially via networks of coupled motions (Liao et al., 2018; Agarwal, 2019; Bunzel et al., 2020; Bunzel et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Liao et al., 2018; Agarwal, 2019; Bunzel et al., 2020; Bunzel et al., 2021.

claim: The active sites of TEM-1 and KPC-2 are surrounded by three loops: the Ω-loop, the loop between α3 and α4 helices, and the hinge region.
source: The active sites of TEM-1 and KPC-2 are surrounded by three loops: (a) the Ω-loop (residues 172–179), (b) the loop between α3 and α4 helices, in which a highly conserved aromatic amino acid is present at position 105, and (c) the hinge region, which lies opposite to the Ω-loop and contains the α11 helix turn (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Glu166 and Asn170 are essential for catalysis and influence the conformation of the Ω-loop.
source: Two highly conserved residues, Glu166 and Asn170, which are essential for catalysis, influence the conformation of the Ω-loop (Banerjee et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Banerjee et al., 1998.

claim: The conformational dynamics of loops surrounding the active site play an important role in enzyme activity and are probably modulated by evolution.
source: The conformational dynamics of these loops play an important role in enzyme activity and are probably modulated by evolution (Pan et al., 2017; Banerjee et al., 1998; Escobar et al., 1994; Guillaume et al., 1997; Leung et al., 1994; Zawadzke et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Pan et al., 2017; Banerjee et al., 1998; Escobar et al., 1994; Guillaume et al., 1997; Leung et al., 1994; Zawadzke et al., 1996.

claim: Differences in the spectrum of activity between KPC-2 and KPC-4 are due to changes in loop behavior.
source: For example, we have recently found that differences in the spectrum of activity between KPC-2 and KPC-4 are due to changes in loop behavior (Tooke et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tooke et al., 2021.

claim: The 1.45 Å crystal structure of TEM-1 in complex with FTA (PDB id: 1PZP) was used as the starting structure for this work.
source: For TEM-1, the 1.45 Å crystal structure in complex with FTA [3-(4-phenylamino-phenylamino)−2-(1h-tetrazol5-yl)-acrylonitrile] was chosen as the starting structure (PDB id: 1PZP) for this work Horn and Shoichet, 2004.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the text with a citation to Horn and Shoichet, 2004.

claim: In the TEM-1 crystal structure, the inhibitor FTA binds between helices α11 and α12, approximately 16 Å away from the active site Ser70.
source: In this structure, the inhibitor binds between helices α11 and α12 (Figure 1a), in a site ~16 Å away from the active site Ser70.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1a.

claim: The 1.35 Å crystal structure of KPC-2 in complex with a coumarin phosphonate analogue, GTV (PDB id: 6D18), was chosen as the starting structure.
source: For KPC-2, the 1.35 Å crystal structure in complex with a coumarin phosphonate analogue, GTV [(5,7-dimethyl-2-oxo-2h-1-benzopyran-4-yl)methylphosphonic acid], was chosen as the starting structure (PDB id: 6D18) (Pemberton et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the text with a citation to Pemberton et al., 2019.

claim: GTV binds in three sites on KPC-2: the active site, adjacent to helix α6, and between helices α2 and α7.
source: GTV binds in three sites on KPC-2 (Figure 1b): the first is in the active site (orthosteric ligand); the second site is adjacent to helix α6 (allosteric ligand 1); and the third (allosteric ligand 2) is on the distal end of the enzyme, ~16 Å from the active site Ser70 in between helices α2 and α7.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1b.

claim: Twenty replicate simulations of 250 ns each were performed for each system, resulting in a total sampling time of 5 µs for each system.
source: In order to sufficiently sample the conformational space, 20 replicate simulations of 250 ns each were performed for each system. This resulted in a total sampling time of 5 µs for each system.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the text describing the simulation methodology.

claim: The simulated systems were considered equilibrated beyond 50 ns as shown by RMSD convergence.
source: The simulated systems were considered equilibrated beyond 50 ns as shown by RMSD convergence.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the text and supported by RMSD data.

claim: The average RMSD for ApoEQ and IBEQ states were between 0.10 and 0.12 nm for all systems.
source: The average RMSD for ApoEQ and IBEQ states were between 0.10 and 0.12 nm for all systems (Figure 2—figure supplement 6).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 6.

claim: The low RMSD values are consistent with previously published results showing class A β-lactamase enzymes to be largely rigid and conformationally stable.
source: The low RMSD values are consistent with previously published results, which have also shown class A β-lactamase enzymes to be largely rigid and conformationally stable when studied on long timescales and rarely divergent from the initial structure (Gobeil et al., 2019; Galdadas et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gobeil et al., 2019 and Galdadas et al., 2018.

claim: At 80%, the core of TEM-1 could be superimposed to less than 0.064 nm for ApoEQ and 0.074 nm for IBEQ states.
source: At 80%, the core of TEM-1 could be superimposed to less than 0.064 and 0.074 nm for ApoEQ and IBEQ states, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 2bi).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2bi.

claim: In the KPC-2 ApoEQ state, the RMSD of 80% of the Cα atoms was below 0.060 nm, while the same subset of atoms had an RMSD below 0.066 nm in the IBEQ state.
source: In the KPC-2 ApoEQ state, the RMSD of 80% of the Cα atoms was below 0.060 nm, while the same subset of atoms had an RMSD below 0.066 nm in the IBEQ state (Figure 2—figure supplement 2bii).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2bii.

claim: KPC-2 is more stable than many other class A β-lactamases such as TEM-1.
source: This apparent rigidity is consistent with the experimental finding, based upon, for example, thermal melting experiments Mehta et al., 2015, that KPC-2 is more stable than many other class A β-lactamases such as TEM-1.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Mehta et al., 2015.

claim: In TEM-1 IBEQ, higher fluctuations are observed predominantly in three distinct regions when compared with the ApoEQ enzyme: in the loops between helices α7 and α8, α9 and α10, and the hinge region including helix α11.
source: In TEM-1 IBEQ, higher fluctuations are observed predominantly in three distinct regions when compared with the ApoEQ enzyme; in the loops between helices α7 and α8 (residues 155–165), α9 and α10 (residues 196–200), and the hinge region including helix α11 (residues 213–224) (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: Binding of the ligand disrupts the hydrophobic interactions within the α11-α12 region, resulting in the opening of the allosteric pocket between helices α11 and α12.
source: Binding of the ligand disrupts the hydrophobic interactions within this region, resulting in the opening of the allosteric pocket between helices α11 and α12 (Horn and Shoichet, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Horn and Shoichet, 2004.

claim: During the ApoEQ simulations, α12 helix behaves like a lid and closes over the empty, hydrophobic, allosteric binding site.
source: During the ApoEQ simulations, α12 helix behaves like a lid and closes over the empty, hydrophobic, allosteric binding site, and thus displays high RMSF at the C-terminal end of the enzyme.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from the ApoEQ simulations.

claim: In KPC-2 IBEQ, more extensive fluctuations than in ApoEQ were observed in the loops between α7 and α8, the hinge region around α11, and in the loop between β7 and β8.
source: In KPC-2 IBEQ, more extensive fluctuations than in ApoEQ were also observed in the loops between α7 and α8 (residues 156–166), the hinge region, around α11 (residues 214–225), and in the loop between β7 and β8 (residues 238–243) (Figure 2b).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 2b.

claim: In both TEM-1 and KPC-2 IBEQ states, interactions of the ligands in their respective allosteric binding sites contribute to enhanced fluctuations of the local structural elements.
source: In both TEM-1 and KPC-2 IBEQ states, interactions of the ligands in their respective allosteric binding sites contribute to enhanced fluctuations (i.e. larger than in the Apo forms) of the local structural elements (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The FTA ligand remains tightly bound in the allosteric pocket throughout the simulations in TEM-1.
source: The FTA ligand remains tightly bound in the allosteric pocket throughout the simulations (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: In KPC-2, the allosteric binding site is shallow and solvent-exposed even in the absence of the ligand.
source: In KPC-2, the allosteric binding site is shallow and solvent-exposed even in the absence of the ligand.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the text based on simulation observations.

claim: In TEM-1, Cα deviations are observed in the loops between α4 and β5, α7 and α8, Ω-loop, α9 and α10, hinge and α11, β7 and β8, and β9 and α12.
source: In TEM-1, Cα deviations are observed in the loops between α4 and β5 (residues 112–116), α7 and α8 (residues 155–166), Ω-loop (residues 172–179), α9 and α10 (residues 196–200), hinge and α11 (residues 213–224), β7 and β8 (residues 238–243), and β9 and α12 (residues 267–272).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the text based on analysis of Cα deviations.

claim: The hinge region and residues in helices α11 and α12 display the largest deviations in TEM-1.
source: The hinge region and residues in helices α11 and α12 display the largest deviations.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the text based on analysis of Cα deviations.

claim: The connection between the active site and the allosteric pocket in TEM-1 in the presence of BLIP inhibitor seems to be mostly due to hinge region motions.
source: This is also in agreement with other experimental data that indicate the connection between the active site and the allosteric pocket studied in TEM-1 in the presence of BLIP inhibitor, seems to be mostly due to hinge region motions (Meneksedag et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Meneksedag et al., 2013.

claim: In KPC-2, prominent Cα deviations were observed in the loops between β1 and β2, α2 and β4, α4 and β5, α7 and α8, Ω-loop, β7 and β8, β8 and β9, in the loop between β4 and α3 leading up to the proximal end of α3, and in the hinge/α11 helix.
source: In KPC-2, prominent Cα deviations were observed in the loops between β1 and β2 (residues 51–55), α2 and β4 (residues 88–93), α4 and β5 (residues 114–116), α7 and α8 (residues 156–166), Ω-loop (residues 172–179), β7 and β8 (residues 238–243), β8 and β9 (residues 252–258), in the loop between β4 and α3 leading up to the proximal end of α3 (residues 94–102) and in the hinge/α11 helix (residues 214–225).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the text based on analysis of Cα deviations.

claim: The most important ligand-induced Cα deviation in KPC-2 is observed in the loop connecting the α4 helix to the β5 strand.
source: The most important ligand-induced Cα deviation is observed in the loop connecting the α4 helix to the β5 strand (residues 114–116).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the text based on analysis of Cα deviations.

claim: A highly conserved aromatic amino acid at position 105 in class A β-lactamases plays a crucial role in ligand recognition via favorable stacking interactions with the β-lactam ring.
source: Mutagenesis studies have shown that a highly conserved aromatic amino acid at position 105 in class A β-lactamases (Tyr105 in TEM-1, Trp105 in KPC-2) is located at the perimeter of the active site and plays a crucial role in ligand recognition via favorable stacking interactions with the β-lactam ring (Papp-Wallace et al., 2010b; Doucet et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Papp-Wallace et al., 2010b and Doucet et al., 2004.

claim: The aromatic side chain at position 105 coordinates the binding of substrates by adopting 'flipped-in' or 'flipped-out' conformations.
source: The aromatic side chain at position 105 coordinates the binding of substrates not only via stacking and edge-to-face interactions but by also adopting 'flipped-in' or 'flipped-out' conformations (Galdadas et al., 2018; Papp-Wallace et al., 2010a; Papp-Wallace et al., 2010b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Galdadas et al., 2018; Papp-Wallace et al., 2010a; Papp-Wallace et al., 2010b.

claim: Loss of β-lactam resistance in strains expressing KPC variants at position 102 or 108 is explained by perturbations that alter the conformation of α3-turn-α4 helix.
source: This explains the loss of β-lactam resistance in strains expressing KPC variants at position 102 or 108, as established in the MIC experiments reported previously (Galdadas et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Galdadas et al., 2018.

claim: 800 short nonequilibrium simulations were run for each system, with a total sampling time of 4 µs for each system.
source: To study signal propagation from the two allosteric sites, we ran 800 short nonequilibrium simulations, with a total sampling time of 4 µs for each system.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the text describing the simulation methodology.

claim: The nonequilibrium simulations were initiated from regular intervals of the equilibrated part of the long IBEQ simulation, starting at the 50 ns time point.
source: The nonequilibrium simulations were initiated from regular intervals of the equilibrated part of the long IBEQ simulation, starting at the 50 ns time point (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: In each nonequilibrium simulation, the ligand was removed from its binding site and the resulting system was further simulated for 5 ns.
source: In each simulation, the ligand was removed from its binding site and the resulting system was further simulated for 5 ns.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the text describing the simulation methodology.

claim: The Kubo-Onsager approach has been used successfully to study interdomain communication in receptors and other systems like ABC transporters.
source: Such nonequilibrium simulations have been applied successfully to study interdomain communication in receptors and other systems like ABC transporters (Abreu et al., 2020; Damas et al., 2011; Oliveira et al., 2019a; Oliveira et al., 2019b; Oliveira et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Abreu et al., 2020; Damas et al., 2011; Oliveira et al., 2019a; Oliveira et al., 2019b; Oliveira et al., 2005.

claim: In TEM-1, the allosteric site is sandwiched between the α11 and α12 helices.
source: In TEM-1, the allosteric site is sandwiched between the α11 and α12 helices.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: The hinge region in TEM-1 has low order parameters indicating high mobility.
source: Adjacent to this binding site is the hinge region (residues 213–218), whose dynamics have previously been examined by NMR and shown to have low order parameters indicating high mobility (Gobeil et al., 2019; Savard and Gagné, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gobeil et al., 2019 and Savard and Gagné, 2006.

claim: The indole ring of Trp229 is sandwiched between two highly conserved residues, Pro226 and Pro251.
source: Located on the loop between the distal end of the α11 helix and β7 is a highly conserved Trp229 residue. The indole ring of Trp229 is sandwiched between two other highly conserved residues, Pro226 and Pro251, present in loops α11-β7 and β8-β9, respectively.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the text based on structural analysis.

claim: The π/aliphatic stacked arrangement of tryptophan-proline is a very tight interaction similar to that observed in complexes of proline-rich motif binding families.
source: The π/aliphatic stacked arrangement of tryptophan-proline is a very tight interaction and is similar in geometry to that observed in complexes of proline-rich motif binding families, including the EVH1 and GYF binding domains, with their peptide ligands (Ball et al., 2005; Freund et al., 1999; Reinhard et al., 1996; Zondlo, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ball et al., 2005; Freund et al., 1999; Reinhard et al., 1996; Zondlo, 2013.

claim: After 50 ps of simulation, the Cα deviations have propagated and can be observed in the loop between β1 and β2 in TEM-1.
source: After 50 ps of simulation, the Cα deviations have propagated and can be observed in the loop between β1 and β2.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the text based on nonequilibrium simulation results.

claim: The loops at the basal pivot of α3 and α4 in TEM-1 responded rapidly to ligand removal and are approximately 33 Å away from the allosteric binding site.
source: Interestingly, the loops at the basal pivot of 3 and 4 also responded rapidly to ligand removal. These loops are ~33 Å away from the allosteric binding site and can affect the spatial position of the turn between helix α3 and α4.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the text based on nonequilibrium simulation results.

claim: In TEM-1, the signal propagates from the allosteric binding site to the Ω-loop via the α7-α8 loop.
source: In particular, the loop between the α9 and α10 helices, which is positioned just below the β1-β2 loop, displays high deviations and forms a focal point for the signal to bifurcate in two directions. First, major deviations are observed laterally toward loop α7-α8 and onward into the Ω-loop (Figure 4a,b).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 4a,b.

claim: In TEM-1, there is a shorter route at the top of the enzyme that the signal can take to go from the allosteric binding site to the Ω-loop, via the proximal end of α12 helix and across the loop between β9 and α12 helix.
source: There is another shorter route at the top of the enzyme that the signal can take to go from the allosteric binding site to the Ω-loop, via the proximal end of α12 helix and across the loop between β9 and α12 helix (Figure 4a,b).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 4a,b.

claim: In KPC-2, the allosteric pocket is shallower and lies between helices α2 and α7.
source: In KPC-2, the allosteric pocket is shallower and lies between helices α2 and α7.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: In KPC-2, the perturbation in the allosteric binding site results in enhanced mobility of the α2-β4 loop, which leads directly into β4 and onward to the basal pivot of the α3 helix.
source: The perturbation in this binding site results in enhanced mobility of the α2-β4 loop, which leads directly into β4 and onward to the basal pivot of the α3 helix.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the text based on nonequilibrium simulation results.

claim: The distance between the allosteric binding site and the α3 helix in KPC-2 is approximately 27 Å.
source: The distance between the allosteric binding site and the α3 helix is ~27 Å.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: In both TEM-1 and KPC-2, even though the point of origin of perturbation is different, the signal leads to common endpoints at the pivot of α3-turn-α4 helix and in the Ω-loop.
source: In both TEM-1 and KPC-2 systems, even though the point of origin of perturbation (i.e. allosteric site) is different, the signal leads to common endpoints at the pivot of α3-turn-α4 helix and in the Ω-loop.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the text based on comparison of nonequilibrium simulation results.

claim: The Ω-loop plays a critical role in ligand binding by altering the conformation of Glu166 and Asn170 which are involved in both acylation and deacylation reactions.
source: The results from the nonequilibrium simulations also correlate well with experimental data, which suggest that the Ω-loop plays a critical role in ligand binding by altering the conformation of Glu166 and Asn170 which are involved in both acylation and deacylation reactions (Chudyk et al., 2014; Pan et al., 2017; Brown et al., 2009; Fritz et al., 2018; Banerjee et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chudyk et al., 2014; Pan et al., 2017; Brown et al., 2009; Fritz et al., 2018; Banerjee et al., 1998.

claim: Dynamic cross-correlation maps (DCCMs) have been previously used to identify networks of coupled residues in several enzymes.
source: Dynamic cross-correlation maps (DCCMs) have been previously used to identify networks of coupled residues in several enzymes (Agarwal et al., 2004; Hester et al., 2019; Agarwal et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Agarwal et al., 2004; Hester et al., 2019; Agarwal et al., 2012.

claim: In TEM-1 ApoEQ, β11 helix shows high negative correlation with β12 terminal helix, representing the lid motion of β12 helix.
